people.name: Diocletian
people.summary: Dalmatian soldier of low birth who ended the 'military anarchy', created the Tetrarchy, doubled the provinces, reformed taxation and coinage, issued the Price Edict, began the Great Persecution and became the first emperor to abdicate voluntarily.
people.detail: His court introduced adoratio (prostration) and a more elaborate sacral ceremonial, though the contrast between 'Principate' and 'Dominate' is now seen as overdrawn. Lactantius, hostile, portrays a fearful, greedy ruler driven by Galerius; pagan sources praise him as father of a golden age. His reforms, extended by Constantine, set the framework of the late Roman state for three centuries.
people.death: natural causes (or suicide, according to some sources) at Spalatum, probably 3 December 311 or 312
scholarship: Barnes, The New Empire of Diocletian and Constantine (1982)
Williams, Diocletian and the Roman Recovery (1985)
Kolb, Diocletian und die Erste Tetrarchie (1987)
Corcoran, The Empire of the Tetrarchs (2000)

people.name: Maximian
people.summary: Pannonian soldier and Diocletian's co-Augustus in the West, who suppressed the Bagaudae, fought Franks and Moors and campaigned in Africa (297-298); he abdicated unwillingly in 305, returned to support his son Maxentius, then turned on him and finally on his son-in-law Constantine.
people.death: forced to hang himself at Massilia, 310

people.name: Constantius I
people.summary: Illyrian officer, father of Constantine by Helena, Caesar in the West from 293; he took Boulogne, reconquered Britain (296), defeated the Alamanni and enforced the persecution only lightly. He died at York after a Pictish campaign.
people.detail: The nickname Chlorus ('pale') is Byzantine. Constantinian propaganda invented his descent from Claudius II.

people.name: Galerius
people.summary: Herdsman's son from Dacia Ripensis, Caesar under Diocletian; defeated Narseh in Armenia (298), was the driving force of the Great Persecution according to Lactantius, dominated the Second Tetrarchy, and issued the edict of toleration on his deathbed.
people.detail: His palace and arch at Thessalonica and his birthplace villa, Felix Romuliana (Gamzigrad), named for his mother Romula, survive.
people.death: illness (probably cancer) in 311, after issuing the edict of toleration
scholarship: Leadbetter, Galerius and the Will of Diocletian (2009)

people.name: Helena
people.summary: Mother of Constantine, of humble origin from Drepanum in Bithynia (renamed Helenopolis), possibly a stablemaid; set aside by Constantius I in 289 or 293, she was made Augusta in 324 and toured the Holy Land in 326-328, founding churches.
people.detail: The legend that she found the True Cross appears only in the 390s. Her porphyry sarcophagus is in the Vatican Museums.
people.death: natural causes, c. 329, probably at Nicomedia; buried in Rome on the Via Labicana

people.name: Severus II
people.summary: Galerius' friend made Caesar in 305 and Augustus on Constantius' death; deserted by his army in Italy, he surrendered to Maximian and was killed.
people.death: killed or forced to suicide at Tres Tabernae, 307

people.name: Maximinus Daia
people.summary: Galerius' nephew, ruler of the Diocese of Oriens and Egypt, the most determined persecutor, who sponsored anti-Christian 'Acts of Pilate' and a pagan priestly hierarchy; defeated by Licinius at Tzirallum.

people.name: Maxentius
people.summary: Son of Maximian, excluded from the Tetrarchy in 305, who seized Rome in 306, repelled Severus and Galerius, and built extensively in the city; defeated and drowned at the Milvian Bridge.
people.detail: Christian sources paint him as a tyrant, but he tolerated Christians and restored church property in Rome and Africa. His son Romulus died in 309 and was buried in the mausoleum on the Via Appia.
people.death: drowned in the Tiber at the Milvian Bridge, 28 October 312

people.name: Licinius
people.summary: Galerius' comrade from Dacia, made Augustus at Carnuntum (308); defeated Maximinus Daia (313), co-authored the 'Edict of Milan', and ruled the East until his defeats by Constantine in 316 and 324.
people.detail: Eusebius, after 324, depicts him as a renewed persecutor who expelled Christians from his household and army; the extent of this is debated.

people.name: Constantia
people.summary: Half-sister of Constantine married to Licinius at Milan in 313; she obtained her husband's life after Chrysopolis and later sympathised with Arius and Eusebius of Nicomedia.

people.name: Constantine the Great
people.summary: Son of Constantius I and Helena, born at Naissus on 27 February; proclaimed at York (306), he won the West at the Milvian Bridge (312), the whole empire at Chrysopolis (324), convened Nicaea (325), founded Constantinople (324-330), introduced the solidus and made Christianity the favoured religion of the emperor.
people.detail: Constantine's religion remains the great question of his reign: Eusebius' Christian hero, Zosimus' murderer turning to Christ for absolution, or a pragmatist steering from Sol toward the Christian God. He killed his eldest son and wife in 326, legislated harshly (molten lead for complicit nurses in abduction cases), and built a dynastic monarchy undermining the Tetrarchy's collegiality. Barnes sees an early and sincere Christian; Drake a consensus-seeking politician; Potter and Lenski stress continuity with tetrarchic government.
people.death: illness near Nicomedia after baptism, 22 May 337
scholarship: Barnes, Constantine: Dynasty, Religion and Power (2011)
Lenski (ed.), Cambridge Companion to the Age of Constantine (2006/2012)

people.name: Fausta
people.summary: Daughter of Maximian, married to Constantine in 307, mother of Constantine II, Constantius II and Constans; she died in 326, reportedly in an overheated bath, soon after the execution of her stepson Crispus.
people.death: suffocated or scalded in a bath, 326

people.name: Crispus
people.summary: Constantine's eldest son by Minervina, pupil of Lactantius, Caesar in Gaul and victor over Licinius' fleet in the Hellespont (324); executed by his father at Pola in 326 for unknown reasons.

people.name: Constantine II
people.summary: Eldest son of Constantine and Fausta, victor over the Goths in 332; as Augustus he claimed seniority over his brothers and was killed invading Constans' territory.
people.death: killed in an ambush near Aquileia, 340

people.name: Constans
people.summary: Youngest son of Constantine, ruler of the West after 340, a Nicene supporter of Athanasius who campaigned against Franks and crossed to Britain in winter 343; overthrown by Magnentius.
people.death: killed at Helena (Elne) in the Pyrenees, 350

people.name: Constantius II
people.summary: Son of Constantine who ruled the East for 24 years against Shapur II, won the civil war against Magnentius at Mursa (351), promoted Homoian Christianity and the Senate of Constantinople, and died marching against his cousin Julian.
people.detail: Ammianus, though hostile to his suspicious court of eunuchs and informers, describes his dignity and self-control; Athanasius and Hilary attacked him as an Arian Antichrist.

people.name: Constantius Gallus
people.summary: Julian's half-brother, survivor of the 337 massacre, Caesar at Antioch who governed violently with his wife Constantina; recalled and executed by Constantius.

people.name: Magnentius
people.summary: Officer of barbarian descent born at Samarobriva (Amiens), proclaimed at Autun in 350; defeated at Mursa (351) and Mons Seleucus (353).

people.name: Vetranio
people.summary: Aged, reputedly illiterate general proclaimed in Illyricum in March 350 to forestall Magnentius; he abdicated before Constantius at Naissus in December and lived out his life at Prusa.

people.name: Silvanus
people.summary: Frankish officer who deserted Magnentius before Mursa, commanded in Gaul, and was driven to usurpation by court intrigue in 355; killed after 28 days.

people.name: Julian
people.summary: Nephew of Constantine and survivor of the massacre of 337, raised a Christian but secretly a Neoplatonist; as Caesar he won at Strasbourg (357) and restored the Rhine, was proclaimed Augustus at Paris (360), attempted to restore traditional cults and died on campaign in Persia.
people.detail: Julian left orations, satires (the Caesars, Misopogon), hymns and letters, making him the best-documented emperor in his own words. His school law and anti-Christian measures earned him the name 'Apostate'; for Libanius and Ammianus he was a hero with flaws. Gibbon and later writers made him a figure of romantic fascination.
people.death: mortally wounded by a spear near Samarra, 26 June 363

people.name: Jovian
people.summary: Christian guards officer chosen after Julian's death; he extricated the army by ceding Nisibis and the Transtigritane regions to Shapur II and died eight months later.
people.death: asphyxiated by fumes at Dadastana, 17 February 364

people.name: Valentinian I
people.summary: Pannonian officer from Cibalae, emperor of the West, who fought the Alamanni (Solicinium 368), fortified the Rhine and Danube, sent Count Theodosius to Britain and Africa and died of rage at a Quadic embassy.
people.detail: Ammianus depicts a capable but irascible ruler who kept two man-eating bears, Innocence and Gold Nugget, near his bedroom. He was religiously tolerant despite his Nicene faith.

people.name: Valens
people.summary: Younger brother of Valentinian and emperor of the East; defeated Procopius (366) and the Tervingi (367-369), supported Homoian Christianity, admitted the Goths in 376 and died at Adrianople.
people.death: killed at Adrianople, 9 August 378; body never found

people.name: Procopius
people.summary: Cilician relative of Julian, commander of the northern army in 363, who seized Constantinople in 365 claiming Constantinian legitimacy; betrayed and executed.

people.name: Gratian
people.summary: Son of Valentinian I, Augustus at eight; won at Argentaria (378), appointed Theodosius, removed the Altar of Victory and ended state funding of pagan cults, and was overthrown by Magnus Maximus.

people.name: Valentinian II
people.summary: Son of Valentinian I and Justina, proclaimed at four; expelled from Italy by Maximus (387), restored by Theodosius under Arbogast's control, and found hanged at Vienne.

people.name: Justina
people.summary: Widow of Magnentius and then wife of Valentinian I, mother of Valentinian II and Galla; a Homoian Christian who clashed with Ambrose over the basilicas of Milan in 385-386.

people.name: Count Theodosius
people.summary: Spanish general, father of Theodosius I, who restored Britain after 367, fought the Alamanni and suppressed Firmus in Mauretania; executed at Carthage early in 376 after Valentinian's death.

people.name: Theodosius I
people.summary: Spaniard from Cauca, made Augustus in 379 to retrieve the Gothic disaster; settled the Goths by treaty (382), made Nicene Christianity the state religion (380-381), defeated Magnus Maximus (388) and Eugenius at the Frigidus (394), and was the last emperor to rule both halves of the empire.
people.detail: His anti-pagan laws of 391-392, his penance after Thessalonica and his relations with Ambrose made him 'the Great' in Christian historiography. He died at Milan on 17 January 395, leaving Arcadius and Honorius under Stilicho.
scholarship: Williams and Friell, Theodosius: The Empire at Bay (1994)
Errington, Roman Imperial Policy from Julian to Theodosius (2006)

people.name: Magnus Maximus
people.summary: Spanish officer in Britain proclaimed in 383; overthrew Gratian, ruled from Trier, executed Priscillian, invaded Italy in 387 and was defeated by Theodosius.

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

people.name: Arbogast
people.summary: Frankish general who dominated Valentinian II, set up Eugenius as emperor in 392 and lost at the Frigidus.
people.death: suicide two days after the Frigidus, September 394

people.name: Eugenius
people.summary: Teacher of rhetoric and magister scrinii raised to the throne by Arbogast in 392; his toleration of pagan senators made the Frigidus campaign appear a religious war.

people.name: Firmus
people.summary: Moorish prince who revolted against the comes Africae Romanus and was hunted down by Count Theodosius.

people.name: Carausius
people.summary: Menapian sailor and fleet commander who seized Britain and northern Gaul, issuing high-quality coinage with Virgilian legends; murdered by Allectus.

people.name: Allectus
people.summary: Carausius' finance officer and murderer, who ruled Britain until defeated by Asclepiodotus.
people.death: killed in battle in southern Britain, 296

people.name: Domitius Domitianus
people.summary: Usurper in Egypt in 297, known from coins and papyri; his revolt, continued by Aurelius Achilleus, was crushed by Diocletian after the eight-month siege of Alexandria.

people.name: Narseh
people.summary: Son of Shapur I who overthrew Bahram III in 293 (commemorated in the Paikuli inscription), defeated Galerius in 296/297, but lost his harem and treasury in 298 and accepted the Peace of Nisibis (299).

people.name: Shapur II
people.summary: Crowned, according to legend, in his mother's womb, Shapur II reigned seventy years; he campaigned against the Arabs, besieged Nisibis three times, persecuted Christians, took Amida (359), Singara and Bezabde (360), repelled Julian (363) and recovered Nisibis and Armenia by Jovian's treaty.
people.detail: He also fought the Chionites and Kushans in the east, incorporating Chionites as allies. Arabic tradition calls him Dhu'l-Aktaf, 'he of the shoulders', from his punishment of Arab raiders by piercing their shoulders.

people.name: Tiridates III
people.summary: Arsacid king of Armenia restored by Roman arms (287 and again after 298), who adopted Christianity through Gregory the Illuminator, traditionally in 301, probably c. 314.

people.name: Gregory the Illuminator
people.summary: Parthian-born apostle of Armenia, consecrated at Caesarea in Cappadocia, who converted Tiridates III and founded the Armenian church; his descendants held the patriarchate for generations.

people.name: Athanaric
people.summary: Leader of the Tervingi who fought Valens (367-369), made peace on a boat in the Danube, persecuted Gothic Christians, was defeated by the Huns on the Dniester (376), and finally came to Constantinople, where he died and received a state funeral from Theodosius.

people.name: Fritigern

roles.t: Leader of the Tervingi in the empire

people.summary: Tervingian leader, rival of Athanaric and patron of Christianity, who led the Goths across the Danube in 376, escaped Lupicinus' trap at Marcianople and commanded at Adrianople; he disappears from the sources before 382.

people.name: Chnodomar
people.summary: The most powerful Alamannic king of the 350s, who defeated Constantius' Caesar Decentius and ravaged Gaul; captured at Strasbourg in 357 and sent to Rome, where he died of illness in the camp of the foreigners on the Caelian.

people.name: Ursicinus
people.summary: Senior general of Constantius II and patron of Ammianus Marcellinus, who suppressed Silvanus (355) and was scapegoated for the loss of Amida in 359.

people.name: Ambrose
people.summary: Son of a praetorian prefect, governor turned bishop of Milan, who fought Homoians and pagans, defeated Symmachus over the Altar of Victory, resisted Justina, forced Theodosius to back down over Callinicum and do penance after Thessalonica, and baptised Augustine.
people.detail: His hymns, sermons and treatises (De Officiis) shaped Latin Christianity; his political dealings with emperors became a template for medieval church-state relations. McLynn shows a supremely skilled ecclesiastical politician.

people.name: Athanasius
people.summary: Deacon at Nicaea and bishop of Alexandria from 328, the champion of the homoousios, exiled five times by Constantine, Constantius II, Julian and Valens; author of Against the Arians, the Life of Antony and the Festal Letter of 367 listing the 27 books of the New Testament canon.
people.detail: His polemical histories created the narrative of a unified 'Arian' party persecuting orthodoxy, which modern scholars (Hanson, Barnes, Gwynn) treat as partisan; his violence against Melitians was the core of the charges at Tyre.

people.name: Arius

roles.t: Presbyter of the Baucalis church, Alexandria

people.summary: Libyan-born presbyter of Alexandria whose teaching that the Son was a created being, subordinate to the Father, sparked the Trinitarian controversy; condemned at Nicaea, rehabilitated by Constantine, he died suddenly in 336.

people.name: Eusebius of Caesarea
people.summary: Scholar of the Origenist library at Caesarea, author of the Ecclesiastical History, Chronicle, Martyrs of Palestine, Preparation for the Gospel and the Life of Constantine; the founder of church history and the architect of the image of Constantine as God's chosen emperor.
people.detail: A participant at Nicaea who signed the creed with reservations, he sided with Arius' sympathisers at Tyre. His works are indispensable but partisan: panegyrical toward Constantine and selective in his documents, though he quotes many genuinely (the Edict of Milan, Galerius' edict). The authenticity and composition of the Life of Constantine, left unfinished at his death, have been debated (Barnes, Cameron and Hall).
scholarship: Cameron and Hall, Eusebius: Life of Constantine (1999)

people.name: Eusebius of Nicomedia
people.summary: Fellow pupil of Lucian of Antioch with Arius and leader of the anti-Nicene bishops, exiled after Nicaea but restored; he baptised Constantine in 337 and consecrated Ulfilas.

people.name: Lactantius

roles.t: Professor of Latin rhetoric at Nicomedia

people.summary: African rhetorician appointed by Diocletian at Nicomedia, who converted and lost his post in the persecution; author of the Divine Institutes and On the Deaths of the Persecutors (c. 315), a vivid but fiercely partisan account of 303-313 arguing that God punished every persecuting emperor.
people.detail: De Mortibus Persecutorum is our only continuous narrative of the Tetrarchy's end and preserves official texts (Galerius' edict, the Milan letter), but its portraits of Diocletian, Galerius and Maximinus are polemical caricatures shaped by its providential thesis.
scholarship: Digeser, The Making of a Christian Empire (2000)

people.name: Ossius of Corduba
people.summary: Spanish bishop and Constantine's chief ecclesiastical adviser, present at Elvira, probably president at Nicaea and leader of the westerners at Serdica; nearly a centenarian, he was forced at Sirmium in 357 to sign a non-Nicene creed.

people.name: Donatus
people.summary: Leader of the rigorist African church that took his name, rival bishop of Carthage from 313; exiled after the Macarian repression of 347, he died in Gaul or Spain. He is credited with asking 'What has the emperor to do with the church?'

people.name: Damasus I
people.summary: Bishop of Rome after the bloody contest with Ursinus, who promoted the cult of the Roman martyrs with verse epitaphs carved by Filocalus, commissioned Jerome's Latin revision of the Gospels and asserted Rome's Petrine primacy.

people.name: Ulfilas
people.summary: Gothic bishop of Cappadocian descent who created the Gothic alphabet and translated the Bible, spreading Homoian Christianity among the Goths; died at Constantinople during a council.

people.name: Priscillian
people.summary: Ascetic Spanish lay teacher and bishop accused of Manichaeism, magic and sexual immorality, the first Christian executed for heresy, by Magnus Maximus at Trier.

people.name: Ammianus Marcellinus

roles.t: Protector domesticus on the staff of Ursicinus

people.summary: Greek-born soldier from Antioch who wrote the last great Latin history of Rome, the Res Gestae, of which books 14-31 (353-378) survive; an eyewitness of Silvanus' fall, the siege of Amida and Julian's Persian campaign.
people.detail: He is generally considered the most reliable and balanced narrator of the fourth century, a pagan restrained about Christianity and critical of Julian's excesses, though his literary artistry and the selectivity of his accounts are increasingly emphasised.
scholarship: Matthews, The Roman Empire of Ammianus (1989)
Barnes, Ammianus Marcellinus and the Representation of Historical Reality (1998)
Kelly, Ammianus Marcellinus: The Allusive Historian (2008)

people.name: Libanius

roles.t: Official sophist (teacher of rhetoric) of Antioch

people.summary: Pagan rhetorician of Antioch whose 64 orations and over 1,500 letters illuminate fourth-century urban society; friend and eulogist of Julian, teacher of Christians such as John Chrysostom, and author of the plea For the Temples (Or. 30).

people.name: Symmachus
people.summary: Pagan senator and orator whose Third Relatio (384) pleaded for the restoration of the Altar of Victory; his ten books of letters document senatorial life.
scholarship: Cameron, The Last Pagans of Rome (2011)
